name: Starling
lede: Starling is a dark, warm grey-brown named for the bird; the books say little about it as a color, but our archive shows how common it is in painting.

sections.title: The bird
sections.body:
The name is a bird's, and the books never define a color called starling [1]. They mention starlings only in passing. Baty's catalogue of nature's colors notes that Imperial Purple is visible on the feathers of a metallic starling, a reminder that this bird's glossy plumage is anything but plain grey-brown [2]. Jarman likens the black floaters in a damaged eye to a flock of starlings at dusk [3].

So the name is best read as a nature name: a dull dark brown-grey, nearer [[taupe]] than [[charcoal]] [1][2][3]. We find no source for when the color term began, so its origin stays undocumented.

sections.title: A bird in a lighting experiment
sections.body: Birren reports experiments by Bissonnette and others showing that the breeding cycle of male starlings depends more on light than on temperature [4]. In a London study recalled by Solly Zuckerman, starlings living under the lights of Trafalgar Square and Piccadilly Circus were compared with a control group from a wood near Oxford [5]. Neither passage is about the color starling, but both show why the bird appears in color books [4][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is one of the commonest colors in the archive, found in more than one painting in twenty. Of 23,781 paintings, 1,346 hold it as a large enough patch (5.7 per cent), as photographed [6]. Almost half of that mass sits in the shadow range of a painting, and only 6 per cent in the highlights [6]. It is a color of interiors and dusk: the Danish painter Vilhelm Hammershøi has it in 17 of his 50 paintings here (34 per cent), about 6 times the archive's rate [6]. Aged varnish tends to push dark colors toward brown, so part of this is the photograph, not the paint.
